x-m-el-econ-01.title: Simple Interest and Compound Interest: When Is Each One Better?
x-m-el-econ-01.goal: Compare two deposits that differ in both interest rate and interest method using a table, and explain with evidence under what conditions the statement 'compound interest is always better' holds.
x-m-el-econ-01.material:
There are two deposit products where you can put 1,000,000원.
Product A: simple interest, 4% per year.
Product B: compound interest, 3.5% per year (the interest earned each year is added to the principal, and the next year's interest is calculated on that).
The table below shows the total amount (principal + interest) for each period when 1,000,000원 is deposited. The unit is 원, rounded to the nearest whole number. Read each row in the order: period, A, B.
2 years | 1,080,000 | 1,071,225
4 years | 1,160,000 | 1,147,523
6 years | 1,240,000 | 1,229,255
8 years | 1,320,000 | 1,316,809
10 years | 1,400,000 | 1,410,599
12 years | 1,480,000 | 1,511,069
x-m-el-econ-01.thinking.0: Check a claim using the numbers in the table
x-m-el-econ-01.thinking.1: Find the point where the conclusion changes
x-m-el-econ-01.thinking.2: State the conditions under which a generalization holds
x-m-el-econ-01.prereq.0: I have heard what simple interest and compound interest are
x-m-el-econ-01.prereq.1: I can use a calculator to compute powers of decimals
x-m-el-econ-01.prereq.2: How to change a percentage into a decimal
x-m-el-econ-01.s.s1.prompt: Look at the table and choose the statement that best describes which product is better when you deposit 1,000,000원.
x-m-el-econ-01.s.s1.hint.0: Go down the table from top to bottom and mark the larger of the two amounts in each row.
x-m-el-econ-01.s.s1.hint.1: Find the row where the larger amount switches sides.
x-m-el-econ-01.s.s1.o.a: Compound interest earns interest on interest, so B is better for every period.
x-m-el-econ-01.s.s1.r.a: You judged only by the interest method. The two products also have different rates. Compare the two amounts directly in the 2-year to 8-year rows of the table.
x-m-el-econ-01.s.s1.o.b: A's interest rate is higher, so A is better for every period.
x-m-el-econ-01.s.s1.r.b: You generalized from the first rows only. Check whether the same conclusion still holds in the 10-year and 12-year rows.
x-m-el-econ-01.s.s1.o.c: The table only goes up to 12 years, so we cannot say which one is better.
x-m-el-econ-01.s.s1.r.c: Even with just the information in the table, there are things you can say. Separate what you do not know from what you can know.
x-m-el-econ-01.s.s1.o.d: It depends on how long you deposit. In the table, A is larger in the 8-year row and B is larger in the 10-year row.
x-m-el-econ-01.s.s1.r.d: You compared row by row and found where the conclusion changes. This is a judgment that states both the evidence and its range.
x-m-el-econ-01.s.s1.explain: In the 8-year row, A (1,320,000) is larger, and in the 10-year row, B (1,410,599) is larger. So we cannot say that one is 'always' better; the length of time is the variable.
x-m-el-econ-01.s.s2.prompt: Let's also look at periods that are not in the table. B's total amount is 1,000,000 × 1.035^n (원), and A's total amount is 1,000,000 × (1 + 0.04 × n) (원). Check with a calculator and enter 2 different periods n (years, a natural number from 1 to 30) for which B is larger than A.
x-m-el-econ-01.s.s2.hint.0: First look between the two rows (8 years and 10 years) where the larger side switches.
x-m-el-econ-01.s.s2.hint.1: Use a calculator to compute both products for 9 years.
x-m-el-econ-01.s.s2.hint.2: Looking at the result, check one more case to see whether a longer period gives the same result.
x-m-el-econ-01.s.s2.ok.c1: It is a natural number from 1 to 30.
x-m-el-econ-01.s.s2.fail.c1: n must be a natural number from 1 to 30.
x-m-el-econ-01.s.s2.fail.c2: For this period, B is not larger than A. Calculate and compare the two amounts directly.
x-m-el-econ-01.s.s2.explain: For n=9, 1.035^9 ≈ 1.3629, which is greater than 1.36, but for n=8 it is 1.3168, which is less than 1.32. So from 9 years on B is larger, and up to 8 years A is larger.
x-m-el-econ-01.s.s3.prompt: Use the numbers in this table to argue against the statement 'compound interest is always better than simple interest,' and add one condition under which the statement would be true.
x-m-el-econ-01.s.s3.hint.0: Guide the learner so that, even if they compare the two products using formulas, they still quote at least one number from the table.
x-m-el-econ-01.s.s3.hint.1: Check whether the sentence points out that the result changes between '8 years' and '10 years'.
x-m-el-econ-01.s.s3.placeholder: Example: It is not always so. ...
x-m-el-econ-01.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you actually show a case where A is larger, using the numbers you chose?
x-m-el-econ-01.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Is the 'condition under which compound interest is better' connected to evidence?
x-m-el-econ-01.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you think separately about when the rates are the same and when they are different?
x-m-el-econ-01.s.s3.model.0: It is not always so. If the rates differ, with A at 4% and B at 3.5%, then after 8 years A has 1,320,000원 and B has 1,316,809원, so simple interest is larger. If the rates were the same, compound interest would be larger from the 2nd year on.
x-m-el-econ-01.s.s3.model.1: No. Compound interest takes time to catch up with simple interest. At 6 years, A has 1,240,000원 and B has 1,229,255원, so simple interest is larger, and at 12 years B has 1,511,069원, which is larger. Compound interest is better only when the period is long enough.

x-m-el-econ-02.title: Is '30% Off Plus a 10% Coupon' a 40% Discount?
x-m-el-econ-02.goal: Find and fix the mistake of simply adding successive discounts, and build your own combinations of discounts that give the same final price.
x-m-el-econ-02.material: A T-shirt with a list price of 50,000원 is on sale for 30% off. At the register, using a '10% extra-discount coupon' takes another 10% off the current payment amount. Below is how a friend worked out the final price.
x-m-el-econ-02.thinking.0: Find the first wrong step in the solution
x-m-el-econ-02.thinking.1: Fix the error and rebuild the solution
x-m-el-econ-02.prereq.0: How to find a price using percentages
x-m-el-econ-02.prereq.1: Telling a discount rate apart from a discounted price
x-m-el-econ-02.s.s1.prompt: Choose the first wrong line in the friend's solution.
x-m-el-econ-02.s.s1.hint.0: Look again in the problem's description to find what amount the coupon's 10% is taken from.
x-m-el-econ-02.s.s1.hint.1: Find the price step by step and compare it with your friend's result.
x-m-el-econ-02.s.s1.line.3: So with the coupon you can buy it for 30,000원.
x-m-el-econ-02.s.s1.explain: Line 1 is wrong. The coupon's 10% applies not to the list price of 50,000원 but to the already discounted 35,000원. So 50,000 × 0.7 × 0.9 = 31,500원, and the 30,000원 in line 4 is wrong as a result.
x-m-el-econ-02.s.s2.prompt: Build a combination of two successive discounts that makes the final price 72% of the list price. The first discount rate is a% and the second is b%, and both are integers from 1 to 99. Swapping the order of a and b counts as the same combination. Enter 2 different combinations.
x-m-el-econ-02.s.s2.hint.0: First decide what percent of the list price the price is after the first discount, then think about after the second discount.
x-m-el-econ-02.s.s2.hint.1: Write what (100−a) multiplied by (100−b) has to equal.
x-m-el-econ-02.s.s2.hint.2: Try a few values such as a=10, a=20, a=25.
x-m-el-econ-02.s.s2.fail.c1: a and b must be integers from 1 to 99.
x-m-el-econ-02.s.s2.ok.c2: The final price is 72% of the list price.
x-m-el-econ-02.s.s2.fail.c2: The final price is not 72% of the list price. Check whether (1−a/100)×(1−b/100) equals 0.72.
x-m-el-econ-02.s.s2.explain: 20% and 10%: 0.8 × 0.9 = 0.72. 25% and 4%: 0.75 × 0.96 = 0.72. These are the only two integer combinations (not counting ones that differ only in order). The sums of the two discount rates (30, 29) are different from the total discount rate of 28%.
x-m-el-econ-02.s.s2.because.prompt: Pick one of the combinations you made and explain why the total discount is 28% even though the sum of the two discount rates is not 28.
x-m-el-econ-02.s.s2.because.hint.0: Write one line for each change, showing what the price goes from and to.
x-m-el-econ-02.s.s2.because.hint.1: First say what amount the second discount is based on.
x-m-el-econ-02.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Does your explanation include a concrete flow of prices (like 100원 → 80원 → 72원)?
x-m-el-econ-02.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Does it show that the discount is based on the discounted price, not the list price?
x-m-el-econ-02.s.s2.because.model.0: Applying 20% and then 10% adds up to 30%, but the second 10% is applied to the price that has already dropped to 80원, so it takes off only 8원. Based on a list price of 100원, the discount is 20 + 8 = 28원, so the total is 28%.
x-m-el-econ-02.s.s2.because.model.1: The second discount is based on the discounted amount, not the list price, so it takes off less than 10% of the list price. That is why the total discount rate is smaller than the sum of the two discount rates.

x-m-el-econ-03.title: Currency Exchange: Which Place Gives More?
x-m-el-econ-03.goal: Before comparing two exchange offices, sort out what else is needed, and find for what range of the missing number the conclusion changes.
x-m-el-econ-03.material:
Before a trip abroad, you want to exchange 1,000,000원 into US dollars. Today the 'cash buying' exchange rates at two exchange offices are as follows.
Exchange A: 1 dollar = 1,400원, no fee.
Exchange B: 1 dollar = 1,380원, the fee is only described as 'special promotion in progress,' with no number given.
You want to decide which one gives more dollars.
x-m-el-econ-03.thinking.1: Telling needed information from unneeded information
x-m-el-econ-03.thinking.2: Finding the boundary where the conclusion changes
x-m-el-econ-03.prereq.0: The meaning of an exchange rate (원 per dollar)
x-m-el-econ-03.s.s1.prompt: Choose all the information that is absolutely necessary to decide which one gives more dollars.
x-m-el-econ-03.s.s1.hint.0: For each piece of information, ask yourself whether knowing it could change the number of dollars the two places give.
x-m-el-econ-03.s.s1.hint.1: Keep only the numbers that decide how many dollars you get.
x-m-el-econ-03.s.s1.o.a: A forecast of whether the exchange rate will rise or fall next month
x-m-el-econ-03.s.s1.r.a: The question of which place gives more today does not need a forecast of the future. Think about where the numbers used in the comparison come from.
x-m-el-econ-03.s.s1.o.b: The fee rate at Exchange B (how many percent it is)
x-m-el-econ-03.s.s1.r.b: You correctly pointed out the number missing from the comparison.
x-m-el-econ-03.s.s1.o.c: The business hours and building locations of the two exchange offices
x-m-el-econ-03.s.s1.r.c: This is everyday information not directly related to exchanging money. Sort out whether it is information that changes the number of dollars.
x-m-el-econ-03.s.s1.o.d: Whether the two rates are from the same day and of the same kind (cash buying)
x-m-el-econ-03.s.s1.r.d: Rates can be compared only if they are values under the same conditions. If you miss this check, the comparison goes wrong.
x-m-el-econ-03.s.s1.o.e: A budget plan for spending during the trip
x-m-el-econ-03.s.s1.r.e: Knowing the amount you need is different from deciding which one gives more.
x-m-el-econ-03.s.s1.explain: Without the fee rate, we cannot know Exchange B's actual rate, and if we do not know whether the two rates are on the same basis, the comparison does not hold. Forecasts of the future, business hours and a budget plan are not used in today's comparison.
x-m-el-econ-03.s.s2.prompt: Let the fee rate of Exchange B be f%, and suppose that because of the fee the amount you actually pay per dollar becomes 1,380 × (1 + f/100)원. Enter 2 different values of f for which Exchange B gives more dollars than Exchange A. (f is between 0 and 10 inclusive, to one decimal place)
x-m-el-econ-03.s.s2.hint.0: Compare the cost of buying 1 dollar at Exchange A with that at Exchange B.
x-m-el-econ-03.s.s2.hint.1: Calculate 1,380 × 1.01 for f=1 and compare it with 1,400.
x-m-el-econ-03.s.s2.ok.c1: It is between 0 and 10, to one decimal place.
x-m-el-econ-03.s.s2.fail.c1: f must be between 0 and 10 inclusive, and only to one decimal place.
x-m-el-econ-03.s.s2.ok.c2: The amount paid per dollar is less than 1,400원.
x-m-el-econ-03.s.s2.fail.c2: The amount paid per dollar is 1,400원 or more, so Exchange B does not give more.
x-m-el-econ-03.s.s2.explain: If the amount paid per dollar is less than 1,400원, you get more dollars for the same 1,000,000원. Since 1,380 × 1.0145 ≈ 1,400, the boundary is about 1.45%. With one decimal place, 1.4% or less qualifies.
x-m-el-econ-03.s.s2.because.prompt: Based on the values you found, write about what percent of a fee rate at Exchange B you should warn people about, beyond which Exchange A is better.
x-m-el-econ-03.s.s2.because.hint.0: Write what price per dollar would make it equal to Exchange A.
x-m-el-econ-03.s.s2.because.hint.1: See what you get when you divide that price by 1,380.
x-m-el-econ-03.s.s2.because.placeholder: Example: If the fee rate goes above about ...%, ...
x-m-el-econ-03.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Did you check the boundary value you wrote by calculating it yourself?
x-m-el-econ-03.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Is the direction correct (above it, A is better)?
x-m-el-econ-03.s.s2.because.model.0: If the fee rate goes above about 1.4%, Exchange A is better. This is because multiplying 1,380원 by 1.45% and adding it gives about 1,400원.
x-m-el-econ-03.s.s2.because.model.1: If Exchange B's fee rate is higher than 1.45%, the cost per dollar becomes greater than 1,400원, so Exchange A is better.

x-m-el-econ-04.title: If You Raise the Price, Does Profit Really Grow?
x-m-el-econ-04.goal: In a situation where price and sales affect each other, find the combinations of price and sales for which profit is 0 or more, and explain why it does not work when the price is too low or too high.
x-m-el-econ-04.material: A food truck sells cups of drinks. The monthly fixed cost (rent and so on) is 1,200,000원, and the ingredients for one cup cost 1,500원. If the price goes up, the maximum number of cups that can be sold in a month goes down: 'maximum sales (cups) = 1,400 − 0.2 × price (원).' The monthly profit is (price − 1,500) × sales − 1,200,000 (원).
x-m-el-econ-04.thinking.0: Refute a claim with a counterexample
x-m-el-econ-04.thinking.1: Find solutions that satisfy several constraints at once
x-m-el-econ-04.thinking.2: Explain the reason for both ends of a range
x-m-el-econ-04.prereq.0: The meaning of profit = revenue − cost
x-m-el-econ-04.prereq.1: Finding the value of a linear expression
x-m-el-econ-04.s.s1.prompt: The owner said, 'The higher the price, the more money is left per cup, so profit keeps growing too.' What is the best evidence to refute this claim?
x-m-el-econ-04.s.s1.hint.0: The claim is 'the higher, the more, continually.' Check directly what happens when the price is very high.
x-m-el-econ-04.s.s1.hint.1: Substitute that price into the formula to find the maximum number of cups.
x-m-el-econ-04.s.s1.o.a: When the price is 3,000원, the monthly profit is exactly 0원.
x-m-el-econ-04.s.s1.r.a: This value only shows the boundary where profit starts to be 0 or more; it does not tell you what happens if you keep raising the price.
x-m-el-econ-04.s.s1.o.b: When the price is 1,500원, the profit per cup is 0원, so losses do not pile up as you sell more.
x-m-el-econ-04.s.s1.r.b: This is about the low-price side. Its direction is different from the claim 'the higher the price.'
x-m-el-econ-04.s.s1.o.c: When the price is 7,000원, the maximum sales is 0 cups, so even though 5,500원 is left per cup, the profit is −1,200,000원.
x-m-el-econ-04.s.s1.r.c: You showed with concrete numbers that even if the profit per cup grows, the amount you can sell shrinks.
x-m-el-econ-04.s.s1.o.d: If the ingredient cost goes up, the profit per cup goes down.
x-m-el-econ-04.s.s1.r.d: That is true, but it has nothing to do with a claim about raising the price.
x-m-el-econ-04.s.s1.explain: At a price of 7,000원, the maximum sales is 1,400 − 1,400 = 0 cups. Even if the profit per cup is 5,500원, if nothing sells, the profit is −1,200,000원. The claim looked only at one thing (profit per cup) and forgot sales.
x-m-el-econ-04.s.s2.prompt: Make 2 combinations of (price, sales) with different prices where the monthly profit is 0원 or more. The price is in units of 100원, the sales is an integer, and it must be at most the maximum sales.
x-m-el-econ-04.s.s2.hint.0: See whether choosing a price sets an upper limit on the sales.
x-m-el-econ-04.s.s2.hint.1: At the price you chose, work out the minimum number of cups you must sell for the profit to be 0 or more.
x-m-el-econ-04.s.s2.hint.2: Only prices where the minimum required sales is smaller than the maximum sales are possible.
x-m-el-econ-04.s.s2.ok.c1: The price is in units of 100원.
x-m-el-econ-04.s.s2.fail.c1: The price must be between 1,500원 and 8,000원 inclusive, in units of 100원.
x-m-el-econ-04.s.s2.ok.c2: The sales is an integer of 1 or more.
x-m-el-econ-04.s.s2.fail.c2: The sales must be an integer of 1 or more.
x-m-el-econ-04.s.s2.ok.c3: It is at most the maximum sales.
x-m-el-econ-04.s.s2.fail.c3: It is more than the maximum number of cups that can be sold at that price.
x-m-el-econ-04.s.s2.ok.c4: The monthly profit is 0원 or more.
x-m-el-econ-04.s.s2.fail.c4: The monthly profit is less than 0원. It did not cover the fixed cost.
x-m-el-econ-04.s.s2.explain: For p=3500, the maximum is 700 cups, and 650 cups × 2,000 = 1,300,000 ≥ 1,200,000. For p=4000, the maximum is 600 cups, and 500 × 2,500 = 1,250,000. In units of 100원, the possible prices are in the range from 3,000원 to 5,500원.
x-m-el-econ-04.s.s2.because.prompt: Write one sentence each explaining why there is no combination with profit of 0 or more when the price is too low or too high.
x-m-el-econ-04.s.s2.because.hint.0: Write how the profit per cup and the amount sold each change when the price goes up.
x-m-el-econ-04.s.s2.because.hint.1: The product of the two factors must be greater than the fixed cost.
x-m-el-econ-04.s.s2.because.placeholder: Example: If the price is too low, ... If the price is too high, ...
x-m-el-econ-04.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Are the reasons for low and high prices different from each other?
x-m-el-econ-04.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Does each reason connect 'money left over' with 'amount sold'?
x-m-el-econ-04.s.s2.because.model.0: If the price is too low, the money left per cup is small, so even selling everything you can sell does not cover the fixed cost of 1,200,000원. If the price is too high, the number of cups sold goes down, so even if the profit per cup is large, the total profit falls short.
x-m-el-econ-04.s.s2.because.model.1: If the price is low, the profit per cup is small, and if the price is high, the maximum sales goes down. So only in the middle price range can you get past the fixed cost.

x-m-el-econ-05.title: Where Does the Price Stop Moving Up and Down?
x-m-el-econ-05.goal: Look step by step at the quantity demanded and quantity supplied at each price, estimate the equilibrium price, and judge what happens when there is a price ceiling.
x-m-el-econ-05.material: The number of boxes people want to buy per day (quantity demanded) and the number of boxes people want to sell (quantity supplied) of tangerines at a market change with the price of a box. The data are revealed one price at a time.
x-m-el-econ-05.thinking.0: Revise your judgment each time new data arrives
x-m-el-econ-05.thinking.1: Find the rule from a table
x-m-el-econ-05.thinking.2: Predict the result under an assumption
x-m-el-econ-05.prereq.0: The meaning of quantity demanded (amount people want to buy) and quantity supplied (amount people want to sell)
x-m-el-econ-05.prereq.1: Finding a rule in a table (increasing and decreasing by a constant amount)
x-m-el-econ-05.s.s1.prompt: The data are revealed one at a time. Each time, choose the idea about how the price will move.
x-m-el-econ-05.s.s1.hint.0: First compare which is larger at each price: the amount people want to buy or the amount people want to sell.
x-m-el-econ-05.s.s1.hint.1: The point where the larger side switches tells you where the equilibrium price is.
x-m-el-econ-05.s.s1.st.0.info: When the price is 10,000원: buyers want 90 boxes, sellers want 30 boxes.
x-m-el-econ-05.s.s1.st.0.ask: If this price stays as it is, what is most likely to happen?
x-m-el-econ-05.s.s1.st.0.after: At 10,000원, the quantity demanded (90) is much greater than the quantity supplied (30). Many people cannot buy, so the price is likely to go up.
x-m-el-econ-05.s.s1.st.0.o.a: More is offered for sale than wanted, so boxes are left over and the price will go down.
x-m-el-econ-05.s.s1.st.0.r.a: Look again at which is larger, the quantity demanded or the quantity supplied. You read the direction of the numbers in the table the wrong way around.
x-m-el-econ-05.s.s1.st.0.o.b: More is wanted than offered, so some people cannot buy and there is pressure for the price to rise.
x-m-el-econ-05.s.s1.st.0.r.b: You correctly pointed out what happens when the quantity demanded is greater than the quantity supplied.
x-m-el-econ-05.s.s1.st.0.o.c: Even if the amounts bought and sold differ, the price does not change.
x-m-el-econ-05.s.s1.st.0.r.c: If the amounts do not match, either the buyers or the sellers will be unhappy. Think about what happens next.
x-m-el-econ-05.s.s1.st.0.o.d: With data for only one price, no judgment can be made.
x-m-el-econ-05.s.s1.st.0.r.d: Even at a single price, comparing the quantity demanded and the quantity supplied lets you say which way the price will go.
x-m-el-econ-05.s.s1.st.1.info: When the price became 20,000원: buyers want 70 boxes, sellers want 50 boxes.
x-m-el-econ-05.s.s1.st.1.ask: Around what price do the amount people want to buy and the amount people want to sell become equal (the equilibrium price)?
x-m-el-econ-05.s.s1.st.1.after: At 20,000원, 70 > 50 as well, so more is still wanted than offered. The equilibrium price is higher than 20,000원.
x-m-el-econ-05.s.s1.st.1.r.a: At both prices, the amount wanted was greater. Think about whether the price should go up or down where the amount wanted is greater.
x-m-el-econ-05.s.s1.st.1.r.b: Even at 20,000원, the quantity demanded is 70 and the quantity supplied is 50, so they are still not equal.
x-m-el-econ-05.s.s1.st.1.r.c: Even at 20,000원, the quantity demanded is still larger, so the price needs to go up further. This judgment matches the data.
x-m-el-econ-05.s.s1.st.1.r.d: The lower the price, the more people want to buy and the less people want to sell. The direction is the opposite.
x-m-el-econ-05.s.s1.st.2.info: When the price became 30,000원: buyers want 50 boxes, sellers want 70 boxes. So far, each time the price rose by 10,000원, the quantity demanded fell by 20 boxes and the quantity supplied rose by 20 boxes (assume it changes along a straight line).
x-m-el-econ-05.s.s1.st.2.ask: About what are the equilibrium price and the quantity traded at that price?
x-m-el-econ-05.s.s1.st.2.after: At 25,000원, the quantity demanded is 70 − 10 = 60 and the quantity supplied is 50 + 10 = 60, so they become equal. The equilibrium price is 25,000원 and the quantity traded is 60 boxes.
x-m-el-econ-05.s.s1.st.2.r.a: At 20,000원, the quantity demanded was 70 and the quantity supplied was 50. The quantity traded at that price is not 60.
x-m-el-econ-05.s.s1.st.2.r.b: You pointed out the price correctly, but check the quantity at that price using the two values (quantity demanded and quantity supplied).
x-m-el-econ-05.s.s1.st.2.r.c: At 30,000원, more is offered than wanted, so there is a surplus. That value has already been passed.
x-m-el-econ-05.s.s1.st.2.r.d: You found where the two values changing along a straight line between 20,000원 and 30,000원 become equal.
x-m-el-econ-05.s.s1.reflect: At first you could only say 'it looks like it will go up' at one price, but as data piled up the range narrowed to 'between 20,000원 and 30,000원,' and in the end you even estimated the value. Look back at how your judgment narrowed.
x-m-el-econ-05.s.s2.prompt: The government set a price ceiling saying 'you may not sell above 15,000원.' By the straight-line rule above, at 15,000원 the quantity demanded is 80 boxes and the quantity supplied is 40 boxes. What will happen?
x-m-el-econ-05.s.s2.hint.0: Compare the two values at 15,000원 and see which is larger.
x-m-el-econ-05.s.s2.hint.1: For a trade to actually happen, there must be both a buyer and a seller.
x-m-el-econ-05.s.s2.o.a: The actual trade is about 40 boxes, and the buyers cannot get 40 boxes' worth of what they want to buy.
x-m-el-econ-05.s.s2.r.a: You used the idea that the quantity traded matches the smaller of the quantity demanded and the quantity supplied.
x-m-el-econ-05.s.s2.o.b: Sellers are not short of supply, so 40 boxes are left over.
x-m-el-econ-05.s.s2.r.b: Check again which of the two numbers is larger.
x-m-el-econ-05.s.s2.o.c: 80 boxes, the amount people want to buy, are traded and everyone is satisfied.
x-m-el-econ-05.s.s2.r.c: The sellers want to sell only 40 boxes. Think about whether more than the amount sellers want to sell can be traded.
x-m-el-econ-05.s.s2.o.d: The quantity demanded and the quantity supplied become equal, and there is equilibrium.
x-m-el-econ-05.s.s2.r.d: 15,000원 is lower than the equilibrium price (25,000원). See what happens when the price is not at equilibrium.
x-m-el-econ-05.s.s2.explain: 15,000원 is lower than the equilibrium price of 25,000원, so the quantity demanded (80) is greater than the quantity supplied (40). Sellers offer only 40 boxes, so the trade is 40 boxes, and there are people who cannot buy 40 boxes' worth.

x-m-el-econ-06.title: Finding the Mistake in a Break-Even Solution
x-m-el-econ-06.goal: Find the conceptual mistake in a solution for the break-even point, correct it, and explain what happens if you make a decision using the wrong value.
x-m-el-econ-06.material: A handmade soap workshop has a monthly fixed cost of 600,000원. Each bar of soap costs 2,000원 in ingredients and sells for 5,000원. Here is a student's solution for the break-even point (the number sold at which profit is 0).
x-m-el-econ-06.thinking.0: Find the error in the solution
x-m-el-econ-06.thinking.1: Understand the principle and fix it
x-m-el-econ-06.thinking.2: Estimate the result of a wrong decision
x-m-el-econ-06.prereq.0: Telling fixed costs and variable costs apart
x-m-el-econ-06.s.s1.prompt: Choose the first wrong line in this solution.
x-m-el-econ-06.s.s1.hint.0: Find where the value found in line 1 was used.
x-m-el-econ-06.s.s1.hint.1: Work out the profit when 120 are sold to check whether following the method in line 2 really makes the profit 0.
x-m-el-econ-06.s.s1.line.0: The money left when selling 1 soap = 5,000 − 2,000 = 3,000원
x-m-el-econ-06.s.s1.line.1: The break-even point is the fixed cost divided by the selling price.
x-m-el-econ-06.s.s1.line.3: So if you sell 120 a month, there is no profit and no loss.
x-m-el-econ-06.s.s1.explain: Line 2 is wrong. The money that can be used to pay off the fixed cost is not the whole selling price of 5,000원 but 3,000원 per bar after subtracting the ingredient cost. The conclusion in line 4 is wrong because of that.
x-m-el-econ-06.s.s2.prompt: Find the correct break-even point, and write the actual profit (or the amount of loss, if it is a loss) when only this student's answer of 120 is sold. Also write in one sentence why dividing by 5,000원 is a problem.
x-m-el-econ-06.s.s2.hint.0: First write how much money from selling 1 bar can be used to pay off the fixed cost.
x-m-el-econ-06.s.s2.hint.1: From the total revenue of selling 120, subtract both the ingredient cost and the fixed cost.
x-m-el-econ-06.s.s2.placeholder: Example: Since ...원 is left per bar, ...
x-m-el-econ-06.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you check that the number you divided by is the 'money left over'?
x-m-el-econ-06.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Can your process for calculating the loss be seen?
x-m-el-econ-06.s.s2.model.0: Since 3,000원 is left per bar, the break-even point is 600,000 ÷ 3,000 = 200 bars. If 120 are sold, you earn 3,000 × 120 = 360,000원, which is 240,000원 short of the 600,000원 fixed cost, so it is a 240,000원 loss. Dividing by 5,000원 ignores that the 2,000원 ingredient cost has already gone out.
x-m-el-econ-06.s.s2.model.1: The money that can be used to pay off the fixed cost is not the whole selling price but only the 3,000원 left after subtracting the ingredient cost. So you have to sell 200 to break even, and with 120 there is a loss of 240,000원.

x-m-el-econ-07.title: Who Grew Faster?
x-m-el-econ-07.goal: Learn that, from the same table, two different standards, 'amount of increase' and 'rate of increase,' can lead to different conclusions, and write a piece that makes a claim while stating the standard.
x-m-el-econ-07.material:
This table shows the monthly sales (in 10,000원) of two stores, A and B. Read each row in the order: month, A's sales, B's sales.
Jan | 200 | 40
Feb | 210 | 44
Mar | 220 | 48
Apr | 230 | 53
May | 240 | 59
Jun | 250 | 65
If drawn as line graphs, A looks like a gently rising straight line, and B looks like a line that starts low and rises a little more steeply as it goes.
x-m-el-econ-07.thinking.0: Understand that the conclusion changes depending on the standard
x-m-el-econ-07.thinking.2: State the range of a claim
x-m-el-econ-07.s.s1.prompt: Is it valid to say that 'one store grew faster' from January to June?
x-m-el-econ-07.s.s1.hint.0: Using only the January and June values, find how much each store's sales increased.
x-m-el-econ-07.s.s1.hint.1: To account for the fact that the starting sales are different, think about which value to compare.
x-m-el-econ-07.s.s1.o.a: A. It increases by 100,000원 every month, which is more than B's increase (40,000 to 60,000원).
x-m-el-econ-07.s.s1.r.a: This only looked at the amount of increase. It is valid under one standard, but it misses that the starting sales are of different sizes.
x-m-el-econ-07.s.s1.o.b: B. The increase relative to the starting sales is much larger than A's.
x-m-el-econ-07.s.s1.r.b: It is valid under the ratio standard, but you also need to look at how it turns out under the amount-of-increase standard.
x-m-el-econ-07.s.s1.o.c: The two stores' sales are of different sizes, so they cannot be compared.
x-m-el-econ-07.s.s1.r.c: Even if the sizes are different, you can compare them using a method such as ratios.
x-m-el-econ-07.s.s1.o.d: It depends on what you measure with, so you have to state the standard.
x-m-el-econ-07.s.s1.r.d: You thought separately about the two standards, amount and ratio. This is the attitude of stating the standard together with the conclusion.
x-m-el-econ-07.s.s1.explain: The amount of increase is 500,000원 for A and 250,000원 for B. The ratio to the starting sales is 25% for A and 62.5% for B. The conclusion changes depending on the standard, so stating the standard is important.
x-m-el-econ-07.s.s1.acc.0: This is a valid judgment if you state that you are using the amount of increase as the standard. But also think about how the conclusion changes under the ratio standard.
x-m-el-econ-07.s.s1.acc.1: This is a valid judgment if you state that you are using the rate of increase as the standard. But also think about how the conclusion changes under the amount-of-increase standard.
x-m-el-econ-07.s.s2.prompt: A friend who cheers for A and a friend who cheers for B both say this table proves they are right. Using numbers, write one piece summarizing under which standard each friend is right.
x-m-el-econ-07.s.s2.hint.0: First write how much each store increased, using the January and June values.
x-m-el-econ-07.s.s2.hint.1: Divide the amount of increase by the starting value to find the ratio.
x-m-el-econ-07.s.s2.placeholder: Example: By amount of increase, ... By ratio, ...
x-m-el-econ-07.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Are both standards included, and did you say whom each one favors?
x-m-el-econ-07.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Do the numbers you wrote come from the table?
x-m-el-econ-07.s.s2.model.0: By the amount of increase, A grew by 500,000원 in 6 months, which is more than B's 250,000원. But by the ratio to the starting sales, A is 25% and B is 62.5%, so B grew faster.
x-m-el-econ-07.s.s2.model.1: A increases steadily by 100,000원 every month and B increases by 40,000 to 60,000원, so A has the larger increase in amount. On the other hand, from May to June A grew about 4% (240 → 250) and B grew about 10% (59 → 65), so B has the higher rate of increase.

x-m-el-econ-08.title: The Optical Illusion Made by Bar Graph Scales
x-m-el-econ-08.goal: See how the starting value of the vertical axis distorts the ratio of bar heights, and choose a scale yourself that reduces the distortion.
x-m-el-econ-08.material: Last month's sales of drinks A and B were 1,020 for A and 1,050 for B. B's advertising poster is a bar graph whose vertical axis starts at 1,000 and where one tick means 10. A's bar is 2 ticks high and B's bar is 5 ticks high, and the poster says 'B sells 2.5 times better than A!' Below is a student's interpretation of this poster.
x-m-el-econ-08.thinking.0: Find the error in the graph explanation
x-m-el-econ-08.thinking.1: Choose the scale yourself and check its effect
x-m-el-econ-08.thinking.2: Judge when it is acceptable to leave out part of the axis
x-m-el-econ-08.prereq.0: How to read what one tick on a bar graph's scale means
x-m-el-econ-08.prereq.1: The meaning of a ratio (how many times)
x-m-el-econ-08.s.s1.prompt: Choose the wrong line in the interpretation.
x-m-el-econ-08.s.s1.hint.0: Look at how the height mentioned in line 1 differs from the sales themselves.
x-m-el-econ-08.s.s1.hint.1: Compare the ratio in line 3 with the ratio in line 4.
x-m-el-econ-08.s.s1.line.0: The vertical axis starts at 1,000, so a bar's height corresponds to the sales minus 1,000.
x-m-el-econ-08.s.s1.line.1: A's bar is 2 ticks, so it rises by 20, and B's bar is 5 ticks, so it rises by 50.
x-m-el-econ-08.s.s1.line.2: The ratio of bar heights is 50 ÷ 20 = 2.5, so B sold 2.5 times as many as A.
x-m-el-econ-08.s.s1.line.3: The ratio of the actual sales is 1,050 ÷ 1,020 ≈ 1.03.
x-m-el-econ-08.s.s1.explain: Line 3 is wrong. The ratio of bar heights is not the ratio of the sales themselves. This is because the vertical axis starts at 1,000, so the heights are 'the value minus 1,000.' The actual ratio is about 1.03 times, as in line 4.
x-m-el-econ-08.s.s2.prompt: Suppose you redraw the bar graph with the vertical axis starting at s. (Bar height = sales − s.) Enter 2 different starting values s for which the ratio of the two bar heights (B ÷ A) is at most 1.1 times, so it does not exaggerate the real difference too much. s is 0 or more and a multiple of 100.
x-m-el-econ-08.s.s2.hint.0: After choosing s, write the heights of A's bar and B's bar.
x-m-el-econ-08.s.s2.hint.1: Try out what happens to the ratio as you raise the starting value closer to the sales.
x-m-el-econ-08.s.s2.var.s: Starting value of the vertical axis
x-m-el-econ-08.s.s2.ok.c1: It is 0 or more and a multiple of 100.
x-m-el-econ-08.s.s2.fail.c1: s must be a multiple of 100 that is at least 0 and less than 1,020.
x-m-el-econ-08.s.s2.ok.c2: The height ratio is at most 1.1 times.
x-m-el-econ-08.s.s2.fail.c2: B's bar is taller than 1.1 times A's bar. Try a lower starting value.
x-m-el-econ-08.s.s2.explain: If s=0, the heights are 1,050 : 1,020, about 1.03 times; if s=500, 550 : 520, about 1.06 times; if s=700, 350 : 320, about 1.09 times. If s=800, 250 : 220, about 1.14 times, which does not work.
x-m-el-econ-08.s.s2.because.prompt: Explain why the poster's graph misleads even though it does not use false numbers. Then give one case where it is acceptable for the vertical axis not to start at 0.
x-m-el-econ-08.s.s2.because.hint.0: Write in one sentence why the bar height differs from the sales themselves.
x-m-el-econ-08.s.s2.because.hint.1: Think of data where small changes need to be shown in detail.
x-m-el-econ-08.s.s2.because.placeholder: Example: Because the vertical axis starts at ..., ...
x-m-el-econ-08.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Is the reason for the misunderstanding connected to the start of the axis?
x-m-el-econ-08.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you explain what the acceptable case is trying to show?
x-m-el-econ-08.s.s2.because.model.0: If the vertical axis starts at 1,000, the bar height is not the sales but the sales minus 1,000, so a small difference looks big. When you want to look closely at small changes, like body temperature, it is acceptable to leave out the start of the axis, but you must state that in the graph.
x-m-el-econ-08.s.s2.because.model.1: Setting the starting value of the axis high makes the difference between the two bars look exaggerated. It can be left out when the purpose is clear, such as showing the trend of values with small changes, and the axis is marked.

x-m-el-econ-09.title: When the Situation Changes, the Cheapest Choice Changes Too
x-m-el-econ-09.goal: Judge how the ranking of three pricing methods changes when the assumptions about number of visits and length of use change, and check by making your own assumptions.
x-m-el-econ-09.material:
A neighborhood gym has three ways to use it.
Single-visit pass: 8,000원 each time you go.
Monthly pass: 45,000원 a month, with no limit on visits.
Annual membership: 420,000원 at once (usable for 12 months, no refund midway).
Which one costs the least depends on how often and for how long you go.
x-m-el-econ-09.thinking.0: Revise your conclusion when assumptions change
x-m-el-econ-09.thinking.2: Make cases that satisfy a condition
x-m-el-econ-09.prereq.0: Multiplication such as total cost = unit price × number of visits
x-m-el-econ-09.prereq.1: How to convert costs to a per-month basis for comparison
x-m-el-econ-09.s.s1.prompt: The plan will change one step at a time. Each time, choose the method with the lowest average monthly cost.
x-m-el-econ-09.s.s1.hint.0: Put the value of each method on the same basis, either per month or total cost, before comparing.
x-m-el-econ-09.s.s1.hint.1: First find which method's value is changed by the newly changed assumption.
x-m-el-econ-09.s.s1.st.0.info: At first, you go 4 times a month and plan to keep going for a year or more.
x-m-el-econ-09.s.s1.st.0.ask: Which method has the lowest average monthly cost?
x-m-el-econ-09.s.s1.st.0.after: With 4 visits a month, the single-visit pass is 32,000원, the annual pass is 35,000원 per month, and the monthly pass is 45,000원. The single-visit pass costs the least.
x-m-el-econ-09.s.s1.st.0.r.a: You go only 4 times a month, so think about whether you need to pay for the method with no limit on visits.
x-m-el-econ-09.s.s1.st.0.r.b: You pointed out that unit price × number of visits is smallest when the number of visits is low.
x-m-el-econ-09.s.s1.st.0.r.c: The annual pass averages 35,000원 a month. Compare it with how much the single-visit pass costs per month.
x-m-el-econ-09.s.s1.st.0.o.d: It cannot be known from the number of visits alone
x-m-el-econ-09.s.s1.st.0.r.d: The number of visits and the length of time are given, so you can compare.
x-m-el-econ-09.s.s1.st.1.info: Exercise became a habit and you now go 6 times a month. You still plan to keep going for a year or more.
x-m-el-econ-09.s.s1.st.1.ask: Now, which method has the lowest average monthly cost?
x-m-el-econ-09.s.s1.st.1.after: With 6 visits a month, the single-visit pass is 48,000원, the monthly pass is 45,000원, and the annual pass is 35,000원 per month. If you go for a year or more, the annual pass costs the least.
x-m-el-econ-09.s.s1.st.1.r.a: You thought the single-visit pass stays the cheapest even as visits increase. Compare the numbers again.
x-m-el-econ-09.s.s1.st.1.r.b: It became cheaper than the single-visit pass, but also compare it with the annual pass's monthly average.
x-m-el-econ-09.s.s1.st.1.r.c: When you plan to go for a year or more, its monthly average is the smallest. This judgment fits the assumptions.
x-m-el-econ-09.s.s1.st.1.o.d: All three methods are about the same
x-m-el-econ-09.s.s1.st.1.r.d: If you look at the numbers, there are differences. Write what each one is and compare.
x-m-el-econ-09.s.s1.st.2.info: You are moving away in 6 months. The annual membership cannot be refunded, and you still go 6 times a month.
x-m-el-econ-09.s.s1.st.2.ask: If you go for only 6 months, which method has the lowest total cost?
x-m-el-econ-09.s.s1.st.2.after: For 6 months at 6 visits a month, the single-visit pass is 288,000원, the monthly pass is 270,000원, and the annual pass is 420,000원. Now the monthly pass costs the least.
x-m-el-econ-09.s.s1.st.2.r.a: You changed the total cost to match the length of time you go and compared. You also took into account that using the annual pass for only 6 months still costs the full 420,000원.
x-m-el-econ-09.s.s1.st.2.r.b: You kept the choice you had planned. Calculate again what the total cost becomes when the period gets shorter.
x-m-el-econ-09.s.s1.st.2.r.c: Compare the total costs of the single-visit pass and the monthly pass. Check the order of the two amounts at 6 visits a month.
x-m-el-econ-09.s.s1.st.2.r.d: Calculate directly whether the total costs are the same.
x-m-el-econ-09.s.s1.reflect: With the same three methods, the cheapest choice changed every time the assumptions about 'number of visits' and 'length of use' changed. When you state a conclusion, you must also state which assumptions it is under.
x-m-el-econ-09.s.s2.prompt: This time, make assumptions yourself. When you choose the number of visits per month n (an integer from 1 to 30) and the number of months m you go (an integer from 1 to 12), make 2 combinations (n, m) for which the total cost over m months is lower for the annual membership than for both the single-visit pass and the monthly pass. (Single-visit pass 8,000 × n × m, monthly pass 45,000 × m, annual pass 420,000)
x-m-el-econ-09.s.s2.hint.0: For the annual pass to win, work out separately which of the two comparisons gets blocked first.
x-m-el-econ-09.s.s2.hint.1: Once you choose m, the comparison with the monthly pass is settled. Then choose n.
x-m-el-econ-09.s.s2.ok.c1: It is an integer within the range.
x-m-el-econ-09.s.s2.fail.c1: n must be an integer from 1 to 30, and m an integer from 1 to 12.
x-m-el-econ-09.s.s2.ok.c2: The annual pass is cheaper than the single-visit pass.
x-m-el-econ-09.s.s2.fail.c2: The single-visit pass is cheaper than or equal to the annual pass.
x-m-el-econ-09.s.s2.ok.c3: The annual pass is cheaper than the monthly pass.
x-m-el-econ-09.s.s2.fail.c3: The monthly pass is cheaper than or equal to the annual pass.
x-m-el-econ-09.s.s2.explain: (6, 12): single-visit pass 576,000, monthly pass 540,000, annual pass 420,000, so the annual pass is the cheapest. (4, 12) does not work because the single-visit pass is cheaper at 384,000. (6, 6) does not work because the monthly pass is cheaper at 270,000.
x-m-el-econ-09.s.s2.because.prompt: Using the numbers in the table, write the minimum number of months you must go for the annual membership to be cheaper than the monthly pass, and give the reason in one sentence.
x-m-el-econ-09.s.s2.because.hint.0: Divide the total cost of the annual pass by the monthly pass's cost for one month.
x-m-el-econ-09.s.s2.because.hint.1: If a decimal comes out, think about whether you need to round up.
x-m-el-econ-09.s.s2.because.placeholder: Example: You have to go for at least ... months. ...
x-m-el-econ-09.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Did you compare the two total costs directly at the number of months you wrote?
x-m-el-econ-09.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you check which one is cheaper at 9 months?
x-m-el-econ-09.s.s2.because.model.0: Compared with the monthly pass, 420,000 ÷ 45,000 ≈ 9.3, so you have to go for at least 10 months for the annual pass to be cheaper. At 9 months it is 405,000원, so the monthly pass is cheaper.
x-m-el-econ-09.s.s2.because.model.1: Dividing the annual pass's 420,000원 by the monthly pass's 45,000원 gives 9.33…, so up to 9 months the monthly pass is cheaper, and from 10 months the annual pass is cheaper.

x-m-el-econ-10.title: Is There No Way to Lose Money by Saving?
x-m-el-econ-10.goal: Look at the interest rate and the inflation rate together, understand that even if the nominal amount grows the amount you can buy can shrink, and state the conditions.
x-m-el-econ-10.material: A student said, 'If I put 1,000,000원 in the bank for 1 year, the interest is 3% per year so it becomes 1,030,000원, so there is no way to lose money by saving.' But during the same year, prices went up 4%, so something that cost 1,000,000원 a year ago now costs 1,040,000원.
x-m-el-econ-10.thinking.0: Find the hidden assumption in a claim
x-m-el-econ-10.thinking.1: Check that the conclusion can flip depending on conditions
x-m-el-econ-10.thinking.2: Refute with numbers and state the conditions
x-m-el-econ-10.prereq.0: How to calculate interest from an interest rate (%)
x-m-el-econ-10.prereq.1: The meaning of 'prices went up' (the price of the same item rises)
x-m-el-econ-10.s.s1.prompt: Choose the best evaluation of the student's statement.
x-m-el-econ-10.s.s1.hint.0: Think about how much the 1,030,000원 after 1 year is worth in terms of a year ago.
x-m-el-econ-10.s.s1.hint.1: Compare how the price of the item changed using the numbers given.
x-m-el-econ-10.s.s1.o.a: The amount of money grew, but the amount of the same item you can buy shrank, so in terms of purchasing power it is a loss.
x-m-el-econ-10.s.s1.r.a: You told the amount of money apart from purchasing power. You used the price information in your judgment.
x-m-el-econ-10.s.s1.o.b: That is right. The amount grew, so there is no loss in any case.
x-m-el-econ-10.s.s1.r.b: You looked only at the fact that the amount grew. Also look at what happened to the quantity of goods the same money can buy.
x-m-el-econ-10.s.s1.o.c: That is wrong. Tax is charged on interest, so the actual interest is always less than 3%.
x-m-el-econ-10.s.s1.r.c: Tax is not in this problem's information. Work it out using only the numbers given (3% and 4%).
x-m-el-econ-10.s.s1.o.d: Prices are unrelated to deposits, so we cannot tell whether it is a gain or a loss.
x-m-el-econ-10.s.s1.r.d: If you think of using the deposited money to buy things later, prices matter.
x-m-el-econ-10.s.s1.explain: What you can buy with 1,030,000원 after 1 year is less than what you could buy with 1,000,000원 a year ago. 1,030,000 ÷ 1.04 ≈ 990,000, so purchasing power fell by about 1%.
x-m-el-econ-10.s.s2.prompt: Choose an interest rate r% and an inflation rate g% (both integers from 1 to 10). Enter 2 different combinations in which the deposited amount grows but purchasing power falls by 2% or more, that is, combinations where (1 + r/100) ÷ (1 + g/100) is 0.98 or less.
x-m-el-econ-10.s.s2.hint.0: The interest rate being lower than the inflation rate is only a necessary condition. Calculate directly whether the ratio is 0.98 or less.
x-m-el-econ-10.s.s2.hint.1: Choose one r, change g, and watch how the ratio changes.
x-m-el-econ-10.s.s2.fail.c1: r and g must be integers from 1 to 10.
x-m-el-econ-10.s.s2.ok.c2: Purchasing power falls by 2% or more.
x-m-el-econ-10.s.s2.fail.c2: Purchasing power does not fall by as much as 2%. Try raising the inflation rate or lowering the interest rate.
x-m-el-econ-10.s.s2.explain: (2, 5): 1.02 ÷ 1.05 ≈ 0.971, a drop of about 2.9%. (4, 7): 1.04 ÷ 1.07 ≈ 0.972. (3, 5) falls short of the standard because 1.03 ÷ 1.05 ≈ 0.981, a drop of only 1.9%.
x-m-el-econ-10.s.s3.prompt: Write a reply to the first student. Use one or two numbers to say when the student's statement is right and when it is wrong.
x-m-el-econ-10.s.s3.hint.0: Compare by the quantity of goods you can buy, not by the amount of money.
x-m-el-econ-10.s.s3.hint.1: Put the interest rate and the inflation rate side by side and write which one is larger.
x-m-el-econ-10.s.s3.placeholder: Example: When the interest is 3%, if prices ..., then ...
x-m-el-econ-10.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you say whether you gain when the interest rate is larger or when the inflation rate is larger?
x-m-el-econ-10.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Do the numbers you used show the change in purchasing power?
x-m-el-econ-10.s.s3.model.0: If the interest is 3% and prices rise 4%, then 1,030,000원 buys less than 1,000,000원 did a year ago, so purchasing power falls by about 1%. Saving is a gain only when the inflation rate is lower than the interest rate.
x-m-el-econ-10.s.s3.model.1: Having more money does not mean you gained. With 3% interest, if prices rise 2%, then 1,030,000원 is worth about 1,010,000원 in goods, which is a gain; but if prices rise 5%, it shrinks to about 980,000원 in goods, which is a loss.
